items.who: Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777-1855), in a Brunswick schoolroom
items.where: the anecdote's paper trail, collected by Brian Hayes
items.when: legend set in the 1780s; traced in print back to 1856

slides.notes:
STORY (legend set in the 1780s; traced in print back to 1856): The story says a teacher set the class to add every number from 1 to 100, and young Gauss answered at once: pair 1 with 100, 2 with 99 - fifty pairs of 101, 5050. The tale grew in the telling - Brian Hayes traced dozens of versions back to an 1856 memorial - but the mathematics needs no legend. The chapter's gauss program does it both ways: the loop accumulates 5050, and Gauss's closed form agrees without looping at all.
SOURCE: The anecdote's documented trail: first printed in Wolfgang Sartorius von Waltershausen's 1856 memorial of Gauss; versions collected by Brian Hayes ('Gauss's Day of Reckoning', American Scientist, 2006). Portrait: Jensen, 1840, public domain.
slides.take: A loop is honest work - and sometimes a formula beats it

slides.title: Why range(5) stops before five

items.cap: Dijkstra - photo: Hamilton Richards, CC BY-SA 3.0

items: A handwritten 1982 memo: include the start, exclude the stop
Lengths become stop minus start; adjacent ranges meet without overlap

items.label: the memo's promise, kept by range

slides.notes:
STORY (1982-08-11): In August 1982 Dijkstra wrote a two-page memo, by fountain pen as always, titled 'Why numbering should start at zero'. His argument: half-open ranges - include the start, exclude the stop - make lengths obvious (stop minus start), let adjacent ranges meet without overlap, and avoid ugly sentinels. Python follows it everywhere: range(5) yields five numbers starting at 0, and the chapter's consoles show adjacent ranges clicking together exactly as the memo promised.
SOURCE: E.W. Dijkstra, EWD831, 'Why numbering should start at zero', dated 11 August 1982, in the EWD archive at the University of Texas. Photo: Hamilton Richards, CC BY-SA 3.0.
slides.take: Half-open ranges are a 1982 argument your loops obey

slides.title: Loop control
slides.notes:
SAY: Loop control is the set of statements and calls that change the course of a loop from the inside. A loop normally runs until its condition fails or its sequence is used up, but the program can also leave it early, skip a single iteration, or react to what happened when the loop ended.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - LoopControl.

slides.notes:

slides.title: The 1997 twister inside random

items: Matsumoto and Nishimura, 1997-98: the Mersenne Twister
Period 2^19937 - 1: the sequence outlives any lifetime
Python's default generator - and the docs say: not for cryptography

rows: 'Return random integer in range [a, b], including both end points.'
items.label: the module answers, deterministically where it can

items.where: Keio and Yamagata universities, Japan; published in ACM TOMACS

slides.notes:
STORY (1997-98): When the chapter imports random, it wakes a generator with a name like a fairground ride: the Mersenne Twister, published by Matsumoto and Nishimura in 1997-98. Its period is 2 to the 19937th minus 1 - a Mersenne prime - meaning the sequence of 'random' numbers will not repeat within any lifetime. It became the default generator of Python, R and countless tools; good enough for games and simulations, and - the docs warn - deliberately not for cryptography.
SOURCE: Matsumoto and Nishimura, 'Mersenne Twister: a 623-dimensionally equidistributed uniform pseudo-random number generator', ACM TOMACS 8(1), 1998; period 2^19937-1; Python's random module documents it as its core generator.
slides.take: import random wakes a named, dated, published algorithm
